issues.explanation: 'Avoid Night' implies fear linked to darkness/outdoor danger, but there are no Threat items and no memory/trigger content tied to night-time, darkness, or outdoor contexts. For this relief-worker trauma, that strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the least coherent item because it addresses a threat context not otherwise represented across Triggers, Memory, or Negative Appraisals.

Yet the selected Threat items are central, high-intensity PTSD threat responses and are also mirrored elsewhere. This makes Threat functionally active in a way that contradicts the formulation structure.

issues.explanation: Threat: Flashbacks and Threat: Physical Reactivity are tightly linked to the Memory and Triggers nodes, but the formulation specifies no active links involving Threat. Including these as Threat items makes the profile inconsistent with the stated node architecture.

issues.item: Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
issues.explanation: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance and Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Surroundings both imply an ongoing current-danger/threat monitoring pattern, which again makes Threat clinically central despite Threat being fully disconnected in the formulation.

issues.explanation: Triggers: Entrapment: Having no options is the least coherent trigger relative to the rest of the profile. The remaining items focus on moral reminders and nightmare residue, while appraisals and strategies emphasize vigilance, rage, and fear of losing control. Entrapment could occur, but here it lacks a clear connection to the rest of the selected content and weakens coherence.

However, the selected Threat items describe a prominent, connected threat response cluster (flashbacks, strong physical reactivity, concentration problems from reminders), which is difficult to reconcile with a formulation in which Threat has no active links to Triggers, Memory, Negative Appraisals, or Maladaptive Strategies.

However, the selected threat items describe an active symptomatic threat response cluster (strong emotional/physical reactivity and concentration disruption) that appears tightly tied to triggers and memory intrusions. This creates a contradiction with the formulation structure, especially given concurrent trigger and memory items that imply exactly the kind of reminder-linked threat activation the model marks as inactive. The other nodes are broadly coherent with each other and with the trauma type.

Threat has no active incoming or outgoing edges, so it should not appear as a tightly integrated maintaining component. Yet all three selected Threat items are non-specific PTSD symptom/severity indicators rather than a coherent sense of current threat, and they are not meaningfully linked to the active Triggers, Memory, Negative Appraisals, and Maladaptive Strategies pattern.

Threat is structurally isolated in the formulation, but 'Scanning for Danger' is tightly mirrored by both Maladaptive Strategies: 'Checking Surroundings' and Negative Appraisals: 'I have to be on guard all the time,' making threat function as an active linked node rather than an isolated one.

Negative Appraisals: 'I have to be on guard all the time' overlaps almost exactly with Threat: 'Scanning for Danger' and Maladaptive Strategies: 'Checking Surroundings,' which contradicts the formulation because Threat has no active links to or from these nodes.

Threat: 'Negative Emotions' is very broad and non-specific, while the rest of the profile centers on intrusive reliving, moral/entrapment triggers, and vigilance-based coping; as a Threat item it does not fit the otherwise isolated, weakly integrated role of threat in this formulation.

vignette:
Thavisouk Phommachanh is an eighty-year-old widowed South-East Asian man who spent the better part of his professional life applying statistical modelling to humanitarian logistics, a career that eventually carried him, in his late sixties, into one of the most protracted conflict zones of his era as a data analyst embedded with an international relief organisation. He had believed, perhaps naïvely in retrospect, that the distance afforded by spreadsheets and satellite data would insulate him from the worst of what he witnessed. It did not. During one extended deployment, Thavisouk found himself present when a supply convoy was ambushed at a checkpoint. The soldiers manning the post had, without warning or apparent justification, begun beating a group of local civilians who had gathered hoping for food distribution. There was no avenue of intervention and no means of escape - the gates were locked, the radio was down, and the relief workers had been ordered at gunpoint to remain still. He stood and watched. He watched a young man roughly his grandson's age dragged by the collar across gravel, watched the guards laugh, watched a woman cover her child's face with her own body. He could do nothing. That absolute foreclosure of choice - the locked gate, the pointed weapon, the paralysis - became the fulcrum around which everything that followed would turn.

In the months after he returned home to his apartment in the Twin Cities, the memories did not recede as he had expected them to. Instead they arrived with a vividness that stripped away all temporal distance. When the images came - and they came often, cycling with the relentless regularity of a film reel that cannot be stopped - Thavisouk did not experience them as recollections. He experienced them as recurrence. The checkpoint was not behind him; it was, in those moments, exactly where he was. He began waking from sleep mid-shout, the nightmare so thoroughly saturating his body that the transition to waking offered no relief, only a continuation of dread that would linger through the morning hours and colour whatever work he attempted that day.

His work, conducted remotely from home, required him to attend virtual team meetings and occasionally present findings to colleagues. He had come to believe that any unguarded word from him might escalate without warning into something he could not control - that the anger he felt simmering just beneath ordinary conversation might, if he misspoke or was challenged, erupt into something terrible and irreversible. Before every call, without exception, he rehearsed his sentences in careful sequence, sometimes for twenty minutes, sometimes longer. The rehearsal offered a temporary sense of containment but left him exhausted and, colleagues noticed, oddly stilted in collaborative discussions. His contributions, once fluid and incisive, had become scripted and brief.

He had stopped watching the news entirely. Any report touching on armed conflict, civilian harm, or humanitarian crisis carried the risk of pulling him back through the gate. The avoidance was total and deliberate. He was certain the world remained as dangerous as what he had seen - not as a philosophical position but as a felt, bodily conviction. Seated at his desk or walking to collect his mail, he found himself scanning doorways, windows, the movements of strangers, cataloguing exits. His body was perpetually braced, as though the ambush were still in progress somewhere just offscreen. The tension was not metaphorical; his shoulders ached, his jaw was clenched when he woke each morning.

What frightened Thavisouk most, beyond the memories themselves, was what he feared they signified. A man his age, a man who had buried his wife and raised children and built a careful, rational life around data and evidence - such a man should not be coming apart at the seams. He had come to believe that the intensity of his reactions meant something was fundamentally breaking down in him, that the boundary between memory and present reality was dissolving in a way that could not be reversed.

It was his eldest daughter who finally persuaded him to seek help, after finding him one morning sitting rigid in the dark, unable to explain where, in his mind, he had just been. He arrived at his first appointment hoping, above all else, to be told that he was not losing his mind - and afraid, with equal force, that he was.
